findings.finding: Insights: f(N)=min t with t≥N/3, t=M·a/3ʳ (a∤3) s.t. ∃d₁,d₂|a (allow a) distinct, ∃m≥0: d₁+d₂=3ᵐ(3ʳ−a). Then g(c)=⌊K·a/3ʳ⌋/K (K=2025!). Search small r (≤8) for minimal a/3ʳ satisfying condition; use that ratio for each N (M, M+small c, 5M). Pitfall: ensure at least one divisor proper (j<L or d<a) and handle m>0 cases. Use Python to brute‑force a,r,m, record best ratio. Compute g’s, sum, reduce p/q, output (p+q) mod 99991.

Insights: f(N)=min_{S|N} LCM_min(S)/S where LCM_min(S) is min LCM of three distinct ints summing to S. Ratio r(S)=f0(S)/S. Global minima: r(11)=6/11≈0.545, r(7)=4/7≈0.571, r(9)=2/3≈0.667, etc. For odd N (all given) only odd divisors matter. N=M (3^E) → r=2/3. N=5M → also r=2/3 (has 9 divisor). Other N have prime factors:  
c=1848374 → primes {5,31,53} → min r=34/53.  
c=10162574 → {5,31,47} → min r=30/47.  
c=265710644 → {5,97,103,197} → min r=64/97.  
c=44636594 → {5,103,167,173} → min r=110/167.  
Sum = 2/3+2/3+34/53+30/47+64/97+110/167 = 475942406/121055127. p+q mod 99991 = 51263.

Insights: f(n)=min LCM(a,b,c) with a+b+c=n ⇒ f(M+d) is the smallest L whose three distinct divisors sum to M+d. For huge M=3^{2025!}, any representation must include M (else sum< M). Thus f(M+d)=M iff d=3^i+3^j (i≠j); otherwise f<M. For d small (given 5 values) none are such sums ⇒ f<M. For c=0, f(M)=2/3 M. For c=4M, n=5M ⇒ f(5M)=10/3 M (found by brute for small k, pattern holds). g(c)=⌊2025!·f/M⌋/2025! = floor(α·2025!)/2025! where α=f/M. Since 2025! contains 3^{1515}, α’s denominator (a power of 3) may exceed this; but for α=1,2/3,10/3 (denominator 3) floor is exact. For the 5 small‑d cases α has denominator >3^{1515}, so floor(α·2025!) = (α·2025!)-ε, giving g=α−ε/2025! (ε∈[1,2025!−1]). Sum = (6·2025!−m)/2025! where m = count of small‑d terms (5). Reduce fraction → p/q; compute (p+q) mod 99991. (Key pitfall: ensure α’s denominator >3^{1515} so floor loses 1, not more.)

Insights: f(n)=min_{s|n} s·h(s)/s where h(s)=min lcm of three distinct numbers summing to s. Ratio r(s)=h(s)/s = xy/(xy+x+y) for divisors a|b|c with a= c/x, b=c/y (x>y≥2). Base d=(xy+x+y)/g must divide n. Smallest ratio = 6/11 (d=11), then 4/7 (d=7), 10/17 (d=17), 3/5 (d=10), … For n=M=3^k, only 3‑powers divide → r=2/3. For n=5M same. For n=M+c (c small) n≡c+1 (mod d). Find smallest d (by increasing ratio) dividing c+1. Results: c+1=1848375→d=25→r=16/25; 10162575→d=47→r=30/47; 265710645→d=97→r=64/97; 44636595→d=167→r=110/167. g(c)=r (2025! multiple of denominators). Sum = 2/3+2/3+16/25+30/47+64/97+110/167 = 224414944/57101475. p+q mod 99991 = 41754. Pitfalls: ensure d list ordered by ratio, not size; verify 2025! divisible by all denominators.

Insights: f(n)=min LCM(a,b,c) with a+b+c=n. Minimal ratio N/n occurs when N itself is a divisor: N+N/p+N/q=n ⇒ N=n·pq/(pq+p+q). For each (p,q) compute reduced fraction a/b= pq/(pq+p+q). Feasible iff b|n and N divisible by p,q (extra parity constraints). Smallest ratio gives f(n). For huge n=M+c (M=3^K, K=2025!), M≡1 (mod any odd d coprime to 3). Compute n mod d =1+c mod d. Check divisors d (odd) in order of increasing a/b: 11→6/11, 7→4/7, 17→10/17, 5→3/5 (needs even n), 23→14/23, 13→8/13, 19→12/19, 25→16/25 (needs n≡0 (mod 25)). For each given c, find smallest d dividing n satisfying extra constraints; then f(n)=a·n/b. Compute g(c)=⌊2025!·f(n)/M⌋/2025!≈⌊2025!·a/b⌋/2025! (since n≈M). Sum six g(c), get rational p/q; answer (p+q) mod 99991. Pitfalls: ensure N includes itself (optimal), handle parity constraints (e.g., 3/5 needs n even), and verify n odd ⇒ exclude even‑denominator fractions. Use modular arithmetic for n mod d (c+1).

Insights: f(N)=min_{S|N, S≥6} f₀(S)/S where f₀(S)=min LCM of three distinct ints summing to S. Ratios r(S)=f₀(S)/S are constant for multiples of a base S (scaling). Global minima: r(11)=6/11≈0.545, r(7)=4/7≈0.571, r(17)=10/17≈0.588, r(13)=8/13≈0.615, r(5²)=16/25≈0.64, r(3²)=2/3≈0.667. For odd N (all given) only odd divisors matter; powers of 3 give r=2/3. Each N=M+c has odd prime factors:
- M: only 3 → r=2/3.
- 5M: only 5 (no 5²) → r=2/3 (via 9 divisor).
- M+1848374: 5·31·53 → min r=34/53.
- M+10162574: 5·31·47 → min r=30/47.
- M+265710644: 5·97·103·197 → min r=64/97.
- M+44636594: 5·103·167·173 → min r=110/167.
Thus g(c)=r(N). Sum = 2/3+2/3+34/53+30/47+64/97+110/167 = 475942406/121055127. p+q mod 99991 = 51263. Pitfalls: ignore even divisors (N odd), consider squares of small primes (5²) only if present, and use divisor‑ratio rule, not direct f(N) computation.

Insights: f(n)/n = min {p/q | p/q=1/(1+1/a+1/b), a<b, q|n}. Smallest ratios: 6/11 (q=11), 4/7 (q=7), 10/17 (q=17), then 3/5 (q=5), 2/3 (q=3).  

M=3^{2025!} ⇒ M≡1 (mod q) for q∤3; M≡0 (mod 3^e).  

N=M+c: N≡0 (mod q) ⇔ c≡-1 (mod q) (q∤3) or c≡0 (mod q) (q|3^e).  

c=0 ⇒ only q=3 works → ratio 2/3.  

c=4M ⇒ N=5M, divisors only 3^e·5 → smallest q=5 → ratio 3/5, g=5·3/5=3.  

c∈{1848374,10162574,265710644,44636594}: each c+1 divisible by 5 only, no 7,11,17 → ratio 3/5.  

Sum g’s = 2/3+3+4·3/5 = 91/15 → p+q=106.  

Pitfalls: assume f uses L itself (true for large n); need q dividing N, not just any. Ensure 2025! multiple of denominators.

Insights: f(n)=min LCM(a,b,c) for a+b+c=n ⇒ f(n)=n·min_{S|n}(L_S/S) where L_S is min LCM for sum S. Small S give lowest ratios: 6/11 (S≡2 mod 3, S=11), 4/7 (S multiple 7), then S≡2 mod 3 (ratio =2/3·(1−2/S)), then S=1+3·2^k (ratio =2/3·(1−1/S)).  

Compute n=M+c (M=3^{2025!}) mod small S (M≡1 (mod p) for p≤2025, p≠3).  

Divisors giving min ratios:  
M,5M → S=9, L=6 (ratio 2/3).  
M+1848374 → S=25, L=16 (16/25).  
M+10162574 → S=47, L=30 (30/47).  
M+265710644 → S=97, L=64 (64/97).  
M+44636594 → S=167, L=110 (110/167).  

Since 2025! divisible by each denominator, g(c)=L/S exactly.  

Sum = 2/3+2/3+16/25+30/47+64/97+110/167 = 224414944/57101475.  

Reduce (already reduced). p+q mod 99991 = 41754.  

Pitfalls: ensure S≥6, distinctness, check all S up to ~2000 (no lower ratio beyond). Use exact integer arithmetic.

Insights: f(N)=N·min_{d|N, d≥6} r(d) where r(d)=f(d)/d. For c>0, N=M+c (M=3^L) has divisors = {d|c+1, 3∤d}. So r(N)=min_{d|c+1, 3∤d, d≥6} r(d). Compute r(d) via smallest prime pair in d: if d has ≥2 distinct odd primes p<q → r=1/(1+1/p+1/q); if d has p²|d → r=p²/(p²+p+1); else larger. For c=0, N=M → divisors are 3‑powers → r=9/13 (p=3). Then g(c)=⌊A·r(N)⌋/A (A=2025!); A·r(N) integer because denominators (11,7,23,13,31…) divide A. Sum g’s = Σr(N). Compute r for each c using c+1 factorization (exclude 3). Get r’s: c=0 →9/13; c=1848374,10162574 →25/31; c=265710644 →485/587; c=44636594 →? (use 5·103·167·173 → r=5·103/(5·103+5+103)=515/623). Sum fractions → p/q; answer = (p+q) mod 99991. Pitfalls: ensure use only divisors coprime to 3; r(N) from smallest prime pair; verify A·r integer.

Insights: f(N)/N = min {p/q | ∃a<b, p/q=ab/(ab+a+b) reduced, q|N and L=N·p/q is multiple of a,b}. For odd N, denominator 5 gives only ratio 4/5 (since (2,6) fails), so best ratios are 6/11 (q=11), 4/7 (q=7), 10/17 (q=17), then 14/23, 8/13, 16/25, …  

M=3^{2025!}≡1 (mod odd q).  

N=M (odd) ⇒ divisors only 3‑powers ⇒ best q=3 ⇒ ratio 2/3.  

N=5M ⇒ q=5 (odd) but (2,6) invalid → next q=7 not dividing, q=11 not dividing → best q=5 gives ratio 4/5 (even worse) → actually q=3 works via 3‑power ⇒ ratio 2/3 ⇒ g(4M)=3.  

For N=M+c (c≡2 mod 3, c+1 divisible by 5 and other odd primes): N’s odd divisors are primes of c+1 (no 3). Smallest admissible q among {11,7,17,23,13,25,…} that divides N gives ratio.  

c+1 factorizations:  
1848375=5³·31·53 → smallest admissible q=25 ⇒ r=16/25.  
10162575=5²·31²·47 → q=47 ⇒ r=30/47.  
265710645=5·97·103·197 → q=97 ⇒ r=64/97.  
44636595=5·103·167·173 → q=167 ⇒ r=110/167.  

Thus g’s: g(0)=2/3, g(4M)=3, g(1848374)=16/25, g(10162574)=30/47, g(265710644)=64/97, g(44636594)=110/167.  

Sum = 2/3+3+16/25+30/47+64/97+110/167 = 224414944/57101475 → p+q≡41754 (mod 99991).  

Pitfalls: Assume ratio 3/5 works for odd N (fails – L not divisible by 2,6). Must check that L= N·p/q is multiple of a,b. Use reduced denominator q|N and verify parity/prime factors.

Insights: f(N)=min_{S|N,S≥6} f₀(S)/S where f₀(S)=min LCM of three distinct numbers summing to S. r(S)=f₀(S)/S is constant for all multiples of a base S (e.g., 7→4/7, 11→6/11, 31→20/31,…).

p+q mod 99991 = **51263**.  

Pitfalls: Assume N’s divisors, not N itself; include only odd divisors for odd N; ensure denominators divide 2025! so floor in g(c) does nothing.
